task.objective: Design how to deploy this agentic delivery pipeline so that it can be used seamlessly in other repositories on GitHub, Bitbucket and similar hosts, on Windows, Linux and macOS, with a UI or TUI for initial configuration (mapping models to agents), and so that it can also run inside Jenkins and GitLab CI.
task.problem_statement:
What the pipeline is today.

The pipeline is a deterministic state machine written in Python (3.13+, managed with uv). A runner walks one delivery task through grounding, design, scoring, human approval, build, CI and release. The graph (pipeline/graph.yaml), the policy files (policy/*.yaml: budgets, vetoes, scoring weights, data classes, escalation, routing, approvers, and a model registry) and the artifact schemas (schemas/) are human-owned: they change only through a reviewed change, and each run freezes digests of them and refuses to reopen if they drift. Models are untrusted: their output is validated, they cannot approve, change policy, or clear a veto, and every model call goes through a dispatcher that checks readiness, data class, retry budget and isolation, and writes a hash-chained provenance log. Run state lives in a run directory (.runs/<id>: state, provenance, sealed stage manifests, gate records, stored approvals) guarded by a file lock. The command line is `python -m agentic_pipeline` with `validate`, `preflight`, `run {init,step,status,resume,approve,decide}` and `models {discover,test}`.

How it is wired today, as constraints on any deployment design.
- Design uses two independent model families, today Claude (Claude Pro) and Gemini (Google AI Pro), reached only through each vendor's own command-line tool (`claude -p`, `agy -p`) under a personal subscription, signed in interactively. Policy forbids API keys, paid API endpoints and usage-credit fallback, and the runner refuses to dispatch if any of eight credential environment variables is set. Build uses a local model driven by the Pi coding agent (a Node program): Qwen3 8B on Ollama today, moving to Qwen3.5-9B on llama.cpp's llama-server; an OpenVINO Model Server is another local option.
- Every model call runs inside a bubblewrap (bwrap) sandbox that needs Linux unprivileged user namespaces: sealed inputs mounted read-only, one writable directory, no network for the local build worker, a private tmpfs home holding only the vendor tool's OAuth credential file for the cloud tools. The dispatcher refuses to dispatch unless the sandbox, protected-path, network, broker and session-separation checks are verified for the run.
- Human decisions at three points (design approval, merge approval, deploy approval) are documents signed with `ssh-keygen -Y sign` and verified offline against keys listed in policy/approvers.yaml. Each is bound to the exact evidence and to the log tip, so it cannot be reused.
- The runner works on a git repository through plain git plumbing: it pins a commit, extracts the tree and contracts, builds a candidate tree and a local merge branch. It never pushes and never merges on its own. Nothing creates a pull request or merge request today, and no deployment environment exists yet.
- The existing CI is one GitHub Actions workflow (validate on Python 3.13 and 3.14, on Ubuntu). The pipeline's own independent-CI stage (F1) reads policy/ci.yaml and runs the repository's checks outside the sandbox.
- The pipeline has only ever been run on itself: its graph, policy, schemas and the source it works on live in one repository, the one passed as the run's root. Model-to-agent bindings are edited by hand in policy/model_registry.yaml; `models discover` lists what the host offers and `models test` runs live conformance checks.

What is wanted.
1. Other repositories: a team should be able to adopt the pipeline in an existing repository on GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab or similar, without copying the pipeline's source into it and without losing the human-owned-policy guarantee.
2. Operating systems: Windows, Linux and macOS. Several mechanisms above are Linux-specific or assume POSIX tools.
3. Initial configuration through a UI or TUI, mainly to map models to agents (which model plays design A, design B, synthesis, review, build and so on), to see what the host can run, and to run the conformance checks.
4. Running unattended inside Jenkins and GitLab CI, including the human approval points.
non_goals: Deploying the applications that the pipeline builds: this task deploys the pipeline itself
Changing the state graph, the vetoes, the scoring weights or the meaning of any approval
Replacing the hash-chained provenance log, the sealed stage manifests or the signed approvals with something weaker
Choosing which models to bind to which agent: the configuration tool only makes the mapping possible

declared_modules: the command line entry points and the run directory layout
the sandbox launcher and the vendor-tool adapters
the readiness preflight and the model registry tooling
the git plumbing used for pinning, candidate trees and merge branches
inferred_impacts: how policy, graph and schemas are shipped, versioned and overridden per repository
how run state and approvals persist when a CI job is short-lived
documentation and installation instructions for each operating system
excluded_scope: the model providers' own tools and accounts
the contents of the existing policy values
dependency_constraints: Every new third-party dependency in the trusted base needs an explicit reason; prefer the Python standard library
The pipeline must remain installable without root privileges

compatibility_constraints: The human-owned policy guarantee must survive: graph, policy and schemas change only through the adopting repository's reviewed change process, and a run still freezes and verifies their digests
Runs, sealed manifests, provenance and signed approvals keep their current formats, so an existing run directory stays verifiable

Nothing may weaken the isolation checks the dispatcher requires today; where an operating system cannot provide a mechanism, the design must say what replaces it and how it is verified per run, or that the stage cannot run there
security_constraints: No API keys, paid API endpoints or usage-credit fallback: this is policy, and the runner refuses to dispatch when a prohibited credential variable is set
Model output and every tool argument remain untrusted and validated
Confidential source and tests never reach a cloud service
Approvals stay signed documents bound to exact evidence; a CI job or a model must never be able to approve
Credentials of the vendor tools must not be readable by any model process other than the one that needs them

known_flows: the task specification and design proposals go to Claude and Gemini through the vendors' command-line tools
confidential source and tests go only to local models on the same machine
run directories, provenance and signed approvals stay on the machine or the CI storage the adopter chooses

criteria: Compare at least two designs for adoption in another repository and recommend one, saying where the pipeline code, the policy and the run state live
For each operating system, say which mechanisms work as they are, which are replaced and by what, and which stages cannot run there

Specify the configuration tool: its form (UI or TUI), what it reads and writes, how a model-to-agent mapping is validated, and how a changed mapping reaches the human-owned policy through review without the tool writing policy directly
Specify how the pipeline runs in Jenkins and in GitLab CI, including where run state persists between jobs and how the three human approvals are collected and verified
Address the subscription-only rule: the vendor tools are signed in interactively and API keys are forbidden, so say what that means for unattended CI and do not hide a conflict
State the dependencies added or removed, the contracts touched, and the data flows with their data classes
required_tests: A portability check per operating system that the dispatcher's isolation checks report truthfully there
Tests that the configuration tool refuses an invalid mapping and never writes a policy file
A CI dry run that proves a run resumes across jobs and that an approval cannot be replayed
quality_gates: The existing test suite passes unchanged on Linux
Policy drift still stops a run

unresolved_questions: Does an unattended CI run need a model path that works without an interactive subscription login, and if so is a policy change acceptable?
Which hosting platforms must the first release support, and is pull-request creation in scope?
Is a web UI acceptable, or must the configuration tool work over SSH in a terminal?
assumptions: Adopting teams already use git and can add files and a review rule to their repository
Developers' machines are where the vendor tools are signed in
The choice between the designs is made by the human at H1
